query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, thermal ageing drives a diffusion‐mediated transformation from a metastable solid solution to a more stable mixture containing intermetallic compounds, which in turn promotes the formation of a continuous, adherent passivating oxide film that improves the alloy's corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (e.g., an alloy in the MgAlCuZnGd or AlMgₓTiSnZn family) exhibiting a mixed microstructure with metastable solid solutions and a limited fraction of intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Subjecting identical alloy samples to controlled thermal ageing experiments at elevated temperatures with varied duration.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environments representative of operating conditions for corrosion and oxidation testing; ageing temperatures and times chosen to induce gradual diffusion rather than complete recrystallization, while maintaining overall densities below 6 g/cm³.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of metastable phases into stable intermetallic compounds and consequent local elemental redistribution that modifies the surface composition.
generation.mechanism: Thermally induced diffusion in the non-equilibrium alloy promotes the precipitation of stable intermetallic phases. This transformation alters the local chemistry, enhancing segregation of elements (such as Mg, Ti, Zn, or Cu) at the surface, which in turn facilitates the formation of a more uniform and adherent passivating oxide film. This film mitigates further corrosive attack and improves high-temperature oxidation performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-processed samples, thermally aged samples will exhibit a higher fraction of stable intermetallic phases and a corresponding improvement in the quality of their surface oxide films, leading to measurable improvements in corrosion resistance (lower corrosion current densities) and enhanced oxidation behavior (reduced mass gain or spallation under high-temperature oxidation tests).
generation.baseline: The as-processed, non-equilibrium alloy state with metastable solid solution-dominated microstructure and limited passivating oxide film formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for alloys designed with overall densities below 6 g/cm³ and requires ageing conditions that are sufficient to promote diffusion-controlled transformation without inducing full homogenization or damaging the alloy integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise ageing temperatures, durations, and critical element redistribution thresholds necessary to achieve optimal oxide film formation are not fully established, and microstructural control may vary with slight changes in alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples. Retain one set in the as-processed (metastable) condition as the baseline, and subject the other set to a series of controlled thermal ageing treatments at selected temperatures and durations in an environment that simulates corrosive and high-temperature oxidation conditions. Perform detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., XRD, SEM, TEM) and characterize the surface oxide film chemistry (via XPS or similar techniques) before and after exposure. Subsequently, conduct standardized corrosion (electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation tests.
measurements: Phase fraction and morphology of intermetallic compounds versus metastable phases
Surface oxide film composition, continuity, and adhesion
Corrosion current density and corrosion potential
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal ageing does not lead to a statistically significant increase in the fraction of stable intermetallic phases or does not produce a more uniform and adherent passivating oxide film—reflected in unaltered or worsened corrosion and high-temperature oxidation performance relative to the as-processed baseline—then the hypothesis that the diffusion-driven transformation enhances environmental stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the association between thermal history and resultant phases and microstructures are investigated for the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu system. By carefully controlling the thermal processing history of the system, the alloy was extensively evaluated and the following summarizes the key results: When prepared by arc melting and casting, this alloy system decomposes into a primary FCC phase resembling the Cantor alloy and a secondary FCC solid solution phase enriched with Cu. The primary and secondary FCC phases remain compositionally partitioned after high-temperature annealing, with no tendency towards homogenization. However, significant morphological evolution takes place resulting in the formation of a “lava-lamp” morphology that is characteristic of immiscible alloys. To this effect, it is postulated that the system forms a duplex microstructure owing to a monotectic reaction. The work further introduces a method applicable to HEA development, wherein controlled processing conditions dictate the most probable and stable composition. The MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ) alloys developed in this study demonstrated a rare combination of high hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance, which are often mutually exclusive in Mg-based systems. As illustrated in the schematic cross-sections (Figure 9), the TZ alloy exhibited a microstructure containing abundant intermetallic phases (Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25) within a Ti- and Zn-enriched matrix (confirmed by the STEM analysis) and fine oxide particles (TiOx and MgO). In contrast, 4TZ presented a more homogeneous Mg-rich matrix containing solid solution domains composed of Mg, Ti, and Zn, and larger Ti rich regions. The presence of Ti and Zn in the matrix, along with uniformly distributed fine intermetallics, promoted the formation of a protective surface film (observed via XPS), leading to passivation and high corrosion resistance. Although micropores were observed in both alloys (Figure 1), which are typically expected to increase corrosion susceptibility, the corrosion current densities of the alloys remained low, suggesting that the protective effect of passivating surface films and refined microstructures outweighed the detrimental influence of porosity. decision.trend: Early investigations in lightweight, Mg‐containing and related complex concentrated alloys began with induction-melted Al–Mg‐rich systems that revealed a mixed microstructure of metastable solid solutions and intermetallic compounds but did not track how these states evolve. Later, compositionally graded alloys (such as MgAlCuZnGd) showed that local variations in processing yield region‐dependent corrosion and compression performance, while studies on AlMgₓTiSnZn linked Mg content to phase stability and diverse functional properties. In parallel, Mg‐containing systems like MgTiZn alloys prepared via non‐equilibrium routes exhibited improved corrosion resistance through the formation of passivating surface films (e.g., TiO₂-rich layers), suggesting that the gradual transformation from metastable to stable intermetallic phases plays a role. Nonetheless, most prior work emphasized hardness and room‐temperature mechanical testing, leaving open questions about the specific mechanisms by which the diffusion‐driven transformation in the metastable state influences corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
decision.unsolved: A mechanistic understanding is lacking on how the non-equilibrium, metastable microstructure evolves—via diffusion‐induced transformation to stable intermetallic compounds—and how this transformation modulates the composition and effectiveness of passivating surface films, thereby changing the alloy’s corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
decision.lever: Conduct systematic thermal ageing experiments that compare a baseline as-processed (metastable) Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with otherwise identical samples subjected to controlled high-temperature exposure (varying both temperature and duration) under corrosion/oxidation environments. Key parameters would include the duration and temperature of ageing to control the extent of transformation from metastable solid solutions to stable intermetallic phases, combined with detailed post-exposure analyses of phase composition and surface film chemistry.
decision.why: This approach follows from the observed trend that non-equilibrium processing produces metastable structures whose slow diffusion-driven evolution is linked to changes in surface passivation behavior. By directly manipulating the thermal exposure conditions, the experiment would test whether the emergence of stable intermetallic compounds enhances passivating oxide film formation, thus altering corrosion and high-temperature oxidation metrics. A controlled comparison that shows significant differences relative to the baseline (or fails to do so) would directly support or falsify the hypothesized mechanistic pathway.
